commentary.bottom_line: Offline studies suggest that AI tools can attach sources that point to the correct passage in most cases, and clinicians rate such answers as more verifiable and more trustworthy. In one simulation, displayed citations also made physicians more likely to accept wrong answers, and no study has tested labeling of chart-verified versus model-assumed content in live care.

perspectives.view: Nineteen studies test source display, and all are offline or benchmark-based. Two randomized trials measured ratings rather than errors caught. Trust rose from 2.59 to 3.80 with claim-level linking, and verifiability ratings rose from 35% to 84%. Indirect outcomes, small samples, and mixed results in four studies support a low certainty rating.

In a 46-physician simulation, correct answers carried supporting citations more often (87.7% vs 65.5%). When a citation supported an incorrect answer, physicians resisted it 34.8% of the time rather than 92%. Attached quotes fully substantiated 37.1% of claims for one model and 48.0% to 78.8% in two other studies. A displayed source may increase reliance without confirming the claim.

Retrieval tools located the correct source passage in 90% to 95% of simulated cases. One tool failed to retrieve in eight of 100 cases. Two studies labeled general-knowledge answers separately from sourced content, and experts valued that layering. No study tested labels for chart-verified versus model-assumed content inside an electronic health record workflow.

One test, a Chinese-language evaluation of 60 questions, used non-English content, and it enrolled no patients. In hazard studies, all outputs written for low-literacy readers lacked citations and dates, and Chinese-language answers scored low on sourcing. No test of source display included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

Adding guideline retrieval raised citation groundedness from 0% to between 51% and 89% across six models. This suggests the feature can work with more than one vendor's model. No study measured how much clinician time it takes to open and check sources, so the staffing cost of verification is unknown.

In a trial with 127 caregivers, only one of four public chatbots gave source citations. Clinician trust rose when answers linked claims to sources. No study tested whether patients or caregivers can use displayed sources to check answers or to decide when to contact a clinician.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether displayed sources lead clinicians to catch errors before they reach patients in a live deployment. No study tests visible labeling of chart-verified versus model-assumed content within an electronic health record. Trials should measure error detection, automation bias toward cited but incorrect answers, and the time clinicians spend on verification.
commentary.underserved_note: One test used Chinese-language content, but it evaluated questions and enrolled no patients or clinicians from underserved settings. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Hazard studies show that sourcing is absent in low-literacy and non-English outputs, so benefits for these groups remain untested.
